title: Kill Switches, Circuit Breakers, and Canary Tokens

questions.question: An agent can spend safely within budget but still publish the wrong post. Which control family addresses actions rather than cost?
options: Kill switches, circuit breakers, and canary tokens
Provider aliases and semantic caches
Prompt templates and model-version labels
Per-request token caps and monthly spend limits
questions.explanation: Cost caps limit what the agent spends, while kill switches, breakers, and canaries stop or expose unsafe behavior inside that budget. A token limit cannot tell whether a cheap action publishes the wrong content.

questions.question: Where should a kill switch live so the agent cannot disable it itself?
options: In a file the agent edits during each run
In a mutable variable in the agent's own prompt
In the last message of the shared conversation
In a system outside the agent's write permissions
questions.explanation: Keep the kill switch in a system outside the agent’s write permissions and check it before consequential actions. If the agent can edit the file or prompt containing the switch, it can re-enable itself.

questions.question: A circuit breaker reaches the open state after repeated failures. What is the usual next state after a cool-down?
options: Half-open, allowing a small number of probe attempts
Open forever, with no recovery path
Deleted, requiring a new workflow to start
Closed, allowing unlimited retries immediately
questions.explanation: After a cool-down, half-open permits a small probe to test whether the path recovered; success can close the breaker and failure reopens it. Returning immediately to unlimited closed operation can restart a failing path.

questions.question: What makes an effective canary token for an agent workflow?
options: A common file required for every normal task
A real production key that grants broad access to the agent
A fake credential or record the agent has no legitimate reason to touch
A benchmark label hidden from the evaluator
questions.explanation: A canary is a fake credential or record the agent has no legitimate reason to touch, so access itself raises suspicion. A real production key creates actual privilege and exposure instead of harmless detection.

questions.question: An EWMA detector adapts to gradually changing tool-call rates. What failure can that adaptation create?
options: Slow adversarial drift may become the accepted baseline
It necessarily catches every gradual distribution shift
It guarantees a fixed limit never changes
It prevents an agent from editing detector state
questions.explanation: An EWMA adapts to recent rates, so a patient attacker can shift behavior slowly until the detector treats it as normal. A hard limit stays fixed and catches a different class of drift.

questions.question: A sequence reads a secret, writes it to a file, then pushes it publicly; each action passes a local detector. What gap does this show?
options: A canary token always detects every data transfer
A kill switch only works before an agent starts
A circuit breaker validates the meaning of each file
A semantic attack can compose from individually allowed actions
questions.explanation: A semantic attack can combine allowed reads and writes into an unsafe outcome although each local action passes. A canary detects access to its planted bait, but cannot guarantee detection of every ordinary-looking transfer.
